title: Big Blue View mailbag: Roster questions, Chauncey Golston’s role, more
description: The mail’s here! Questions and answers as the Giants open the preseason.
fullText:
Norm Weiss asks: Ed, I'm sure you haven't been overwhelmed with Damon Bankston questions. Have you seen enough from him to see him making the 53 man roster? I live in New Mexico and had the pleasure of seeing him play at UNM. His play strength and speed are much greater than his measurables. He is an explosive athlete, as seen by his 2 returns for touchdowns last year on only 12 returns. He can run surprisingly well between the tackles as well as outside due to his short distance quickness and vision. He is also a good receiver out of the backfield. BTW, he led the Texas 5A division in rushing yards as a high school senior. I think he and Banks would make a dynamic kick return duo. Do you think he has a chance?

Ed says: Norm, all I can really go by is the distribution of practice reps. Bankston gets a few second-team reps, and a lot of third-team reps. He hasn't really stood out. Unless that changes, he is not making the 53-man roster. John Harbaugh said the other day that he likes Bankston's talent, but that Bankston is behind the other backs in terms of his understanding of the offense.

Ed Helinski asks: Have the Giants indicated that they'll return to West Virginia for training camp in 2027? Instead, how about having camp at SUNY Cortland and its excellent facilities? The Jets held camp there from 2009-2014.

Ed says: The Giants did not build their own practice facility, and they aren't spending millions of dollars now to renovate it, to spend additional money moving training camp to a remote location.

As far as I know, they plan to train in East Rutherford next summer. That would only change if something construction-related made that unworkable. If they had to move, The Greenbrier would likely be their first choice. It has everything, with the exception of an indoor practice bubble.

Michael Spina asks: If you could ask Harbaugh any question at all about this team, and he had to answer it as fully and truthfully as possible, what would you ask him?

Ed says: Michael, I don't think I would ask him a question about this team at all. I think I might ask him a question about legacy. No head coach has ever won a Super Bowl with two teams. I think I would ask him how much it would mean to him to be the first, and whether or not he would consider his tenure with the Giants a success if he does not at least get the team to a Super Bowl at some point.

Thomas Shelby asks: Are the Giants allowed to practice in Met Life Stadium?

Ed says: Thomas, yes, they are "allowed" to. I have seen them do it on occasion over the years. But, NFL teams do not generally practice in their home stadiums. They have practice facilities for that where they have locker room, practice bubbles, meeting rooms, weight rooms, and all of their equipment.

The Giants' facility is on the other side of the Meadowlands Sports Complex parking lot. The conditions are the same. In terms of home field advantage, that is created by the fans. It takes playing good football, getting fans excited, filling the stadium with your own fans rather than fans of the opposing team. The Giants have not played enough good football in recent years to make that happen.

Joseph Rivage asks: Hi Ed, my question regards Jaxson Dart. Like many others last season, I saw a QB with potential franchise ability. It looked like they finally got "the guy". So far this season though it seems like he's struggling a little with fitting into the new system that Nagy is implementing. Do you think there's a cause for concern or is it just growing pains for a young player adjusting to this new system and by extension the offense as a whole?

Ed says: Joseph, what gives anyone the idea that Dart is "struggling"? The offense is learning an entirely new system from the ground up. It is normal that offenses are behind defenses at the beginning, especially in a circumstance like this. The reality is that an offensive install is far more cumbersome and complicated than a defensive one.

Dart has, to my eyes, looked fine. He has been comfortable under center. He is learning new things. That's how you grow as a player. It's practice, and it isn't supposed to be perfect. It's supposed to be hard.

Don't get yourself all tied up in knots about anything you read or hear from the daily practice reports.

Steve Goodyear asks: Thoughts on Kubas? Can he play a viable backup center? Does he make the roster?

Ed says: Steve, I doubt Jake Kubas is making the roster. He worked all spring and summer as a third-team guard, until the injuries to John Michael Schmitz and Lucas Patrick forced him to take reps at center over the past week.

With practice reps and preseason playing time, though, comes an opportunity. So, I won't say it is impossible for Kubas to make the roster. Just unlikely.

Matthew Burns asks: What can you tell us about the Giants' Strength & Conditioning/Performance Staff? Are they new to the G-Men? Were any of the coaches with Harbaugh in Baltimore?

Ed says: Matthew, not much, to be honest. The Giants' official website lists nine members of that staff. Aaron Wellman, Sam Coad, Drew Wilson, and Matthew Frakes are holdovers. Sam Rosengarten, Chris Allen, and Ron Shrift come from the Ravens. Mark Naylor comes from the Arizona Cardinals. Brian Ellis worked in Baltimore for a couple of years, but was most recently at Baylor.

Henry Jacukiewicz asks: Ed, my question is about Chauncey Golston. What do you see as his role ? I thought he was a good pickup but he seems to have faded into the background.

Ed says: Henry, Golston is a good player who lost playing time last season after the Giants were able to draft Abdul Carter. He also dealt with injuries and played in only 10 games.

Golston will be the fourth edge defender, and will play in some situations as a hand in the ground defensive end. He is nice depth to have because he can fill a number of different roles when needed.

Jeffrey Smith asks: Hi Ed, have not heard a peep about either Jack Kelly or Chauncey Golston this summer. any comments about either of them? BTW, I think Jack Kelly is a great name for a NY Giant LB.

Ed says: Jeffrey, see above for thoughts on Golston. As for Kelly, we have written about him a number of times. He is playing with the second team ahead of Darius Muasau, and has had a nice camp. He has shown surprising range in coverage, and should be a nice backup.

ctscan123 asks: Anyone on the roster bubble that we could maybe swing a trade for rather than cut? Only name that comes to mind is Ben Sauls… Think we could get anything for him? Anyone else?

Ed says: CT, here is the problem with trading players at the deadline. There are 32 teams cutting their rosters from 90 players to 53. That's 1,184 players who are going to lose their jobs, meaning they will be available to other teams. Unless a team really loves one particular player, there are going to be a plethora of players available at every position via the waiver wire or free agency.

It is very difficult to get anything for a player another team knows you don't have room for and are about to cut. It happens occasionally, and I'm sure GM Joe Schoen will look for opportunities, but they aren't easy to find.

David Clancy asks: Curious about the WR competition. I know you've been doing the 53 man roster predictions as lock, bubble, longshot but I'm curious about 1. What you think harbaugh and Co. Will do? (I.e what you think will happen) 2. What you would do?

Ed says: David, there are three preseason games and a lot of practices to be held before that decision has to be made. I am not going to answer it today, because all of the evidence has not yet been collected and the answer could be different in three weeks. I will answer that when I make my final 53-man roster projection.

Dave Nelson asks: What are biggest differences in the way training camp and/or practices are being run between Harbaugh and previous coaching regimes (Shurmur, Judge, Daboll)? Do you sense a different level of player engagement or buy-in?

Ed says: Dave, if you have been reading the practice reports here and in other places, you should know the answer to this one. It is a different, faster pace, a different intensity. More padded work (within the rules of the CBA). No short days. Even the job-throughs last a full 2½ hours. The players are bought-in because they want to win, and they know Harbaugh's track record.

Steve Alessandrini asks: I know our natural inclination as fans is to focus on the tangible things – how many passes Dart completes in practice, how Nabers is looking in drills, the O line depth, etc. And there has been lots written about that. But those things all come down to the talent level of the team. And while no one is arguing the Giants could have used more talent the last 10 years, I don't think that's why the team has struggled for most of the last decade. They lacked a winning culture and identity. From the time you have been around the team, how are the "vibes" on that front?

Ed says: Steve, all I can say on that front is this group of players understands that things have been bad for the Giants, and that John Harbaugh has done a lot of winning. They want to win. The vibes are good. Of course, vibes don't get you wins. Talent and execution get you wins.

Bob Conyea asks: Ed, I suppose we will soon be saying goodbye to Evan Neal and Jalin Hyatt. No ill will for either player, or Joe Schoen for drafting them. But my question is why are they still here? Are there financial reasons beyond Neal's rookie contract? An unwillingness to simply admit to a mistake and move on? I contrast this with the bubble and long shot players busting their tails just to make the team. Whether on special teams or in a backup role, they stand a better chance of making a contribution during the season than failed draft picks who are healthy scratches. What is your opinion on this?

Ed says: Bob, Jalin Hyatt is on the final year of his rookie contract. Evan Neal is not. He is on a one-year deal that does not have a single guaranteed dollar. If he does not make the team, the Giants won't owe him a penny

For Hyatt, he is still on that rookie deal, so why wouldn't the Giants bring him to camp? If he doesn't make it, so bit it. At least this coaching staff will have gotten a look at him.

In terms of Neal, you have to remember that almost everyone thought Neal was worthy of a top 10 pick and would be a stud offensive lineman. He is in camp because Harbaugh knows what the Ravens thought of Neal before the draft, and he wants to see for himself if there is anything there.

As I was told during the offseason, you can bring an undrafted free agent to training camp who you know has zero chance to make the team, or you can bring a former first-round pick. The Giants chose the former first-round pick.

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

title: Gabriel Bortoleto expects long-term stay at Audi's F1 team
description: The Brazilian sophomore is excited by the German manufacturer's long-term prospects in F1
fullText:
Gabriel Bortoleto expects to remain at Audi for the long-term, stating that he has a deal with the Swiss-German Formula 1 outfit to cover the next few seasons.

The Brazilian joined the team in 2025 for its final season as Sauber and scored 19 points in his rookie year, and across 2026 has scored 10 of Audi's 12 points. As it stands, he sits 14th in the championship - eight points behind Haas' Oliver Bearman.

His Belgian Grand Prix was arguably the highlight of the season so far, when he qualified ninth on a circuit where Audi had expected to struggle, given its power deficit versus the other top-line manufacturers. After starting eighth thanks to Lando Norris' grid penalty, Bortoleto held onto his position and stalled out a late charge from Arvid Lindblad to secure four points.

With Audi enduring something of a learning season as it adapts to life as an F1 manufacturer team, Bortoleto says that he retains belief in the team's long-term ambitions. Speaking to Motorsport.com's Brazilian edition, the Paulista said that he remains tied to the team for the next few years.

"As far as I can say, because it's something confidential, let's just say there are no clauses. I have a long-term contract with Audi. I've already said it: I'll be with Audi next year, and not only next year, but for the following years as well," Bortoleto said.

"The intention, and I've always said this from the beginning, is that this is a long-term project. Mattia [Binotto] is always talking about 2030. So let's put it that way. It's a project we really believe in. I believed in it when I joined them, they believe in my potential, and that's what I can say. It's something long-term.

"I'm very excited. This year was the first step, building a new car and a new engine. Next year will be another step, and then we'll be able to start putting things into practice."

Bortoleto admitted that it was not entirely clear if his team-mate Nico Hulkenberg had a contract for next year as well, but he was keen to outline that he hugely enjoys working with the veteran German driver.

The two have developed a good working relationship, and Bortoleto has demonstrated across the past 18 months that he can match his elder team-mate for pace.

"I can say that my seat is secured. I'm not going to talk about other people's contracts, but I really enjoy working with Nico," he added.

"That's something I want to say and make very clear. He's a guy I really like. He's fast, experienced and brings a lot of positive things to the team, and we'll see what the future holds.

"But I'm happy. I believe in myself and I believe in my potential."

Speaking about his own development, Bortoleto felt that he had grown significantly as a driver since making his debut last season. On winning 2024's Formula 2 title at the first time of asking, Bortoleto was in demand - and Sauber/Audi agreed to spring him from his McLaren development deal to drive in 2025.

Since he'd only been part of McLaren's driver development programme for a year, he'd had very few opportunities to drive an F1 car; his TPC  [Testing of Previous Cars] run in Austria in 2024 being his only meaningful run before jumping into the Sauber in Abu Dhabi's post-season test.

Bortoleto felt that he was "very raw" when he got to F1, and was thrust upon a steep development curve through the opening phase of 2025.

"[I'm] totally different. I arrived in F1 very raw. Everything happened very quickly. My opportunity in F1 came from one moment to the next. I had barely done any testing, not even TPC.

"I basically had to go straight into an F1 season, do pre-season testing in Bahrain, and that was it. So the amount I learned throughout the year was huge. I'm still learning a lot. I've had a team that has supported me all the way.

"We had some great moments last year. So far this year, I'm also very happy with my season. We've achieved a lot of things together and we're making the car more and more competitive."

title: How Texas high jumper Osawese Agbonkonkon wants to clear the bar as a sci-fi author
description: Texas track athlete Osawese Agbonkonkon is leaping into the world of sci-fi.
fullText:
The images play through Osawese Agbonkonkon's mind, flashing of all the things he'd done since that fateful moment the trajectory of his life changed.

His first time competing in the high jump as a raw junior varsity athlete whose best height was good enough to win the varsity competition. The first time he told the high school track coach "No" after being spotted dunking a basketball in the warm-up line -- and all the subsequent "Nos" before finally giving in. The NCAA Div. I outdoor track and field championships. The SEC and Pac-12 championships. The ongoing press hits to promote his sci-fi novel.

How much different would his life be if not for that high school coach's persistence?

"If I never picked up track and field, I'm never here. We're never having this conversation," Agbonkonkon told For The Win in a recent interview. "More than likely, I'm not at the University of Texas competing as an athlete. I mean, the book still would have been a thing because I've been writing that since long before track and field was ever in the picture. But the response, the way that it's changed the whole story around me as a person who is an athlete, who's an author, who does all these things, I don't think any of that happens if I don't take him up on that offer."

Now that he's here, Agbonkonkon isn't leaving the rest up to chance.

If becoming a student-athlete with increased visibility as an author was the result of the Texas native's good fortune -- being in the right place at the right time -- the rest of his story won't be. Agbonkonkon has it all mapped out from here. He's attempting to build a world on the foundation of his self-published 2024 debut novel Psychic Suit, a sci-fi thriller about an enhanced group of humans called The Psychics.

"I'm out here planning strategies," Agbonkonkon said, detailing his masterplan of building a universe around the book. "I have dozens of documents open of the strategy we're executing. This is how I expect it to go."

Part of that strategy is bringing The Psychics to Hollywood. Agbonkonkon said a TV bible for Psychic Suit is being shopped to studios. If picked up, it'll be the next item checked off from a dream that's been years in the making.

Before he was a collegiate high jumper, Agbonkonkon was being prepped for the opportunity ahead of him without knowing it. He caught the writing bug in the fifth grade from a standardized test question he couldn't get out of his head when he went home and wrote his first cohesive story. Inspired by Marvel's Captain America movies, James Bond and the Fast & Furious series, Agbonkonkon had the idea for a Psychic Suit series a couple of years later. In 2018, he finally put pen to paper, churning out the first three books of the series, which left plenty time for revisions before his 2024 debut. Now a rising college senior, Agbonkonkon is targeting the end of 2026 to release the second book.

But there's plenty on the bulletin board before then. Acting as his own publicist, Agbonkonkon is still doing legwork to increase visibility of the first book. He's also still a student… and an athlete. And he's not happy with how last season ended, even after making it to nationals in June.

"I was injured essentially the whole season, so it did not go as planned," said Agbonkonkon, who placed 16th in the NCAA high jump championships. "But going into next year, I definitely want to get healthy and am working on that right now. So I'm confident that if we're healthy that we can have a nice offseason going into this senior year and make some waves in the NCAA."

And yes, he plans to go pro as a high jumper too.

If it sounds like Agbonkonkon is doing a lot, it's because he is. But none of the many hats he's wearing takes priority over the other. He believes he can do them all, because of the support of his family, coaches and athletic staff, along with -- as he put it -- "Why not you? ... There's really not a reason you can't."

That's not to say the balance is easy. Sacrifices are necessary, and often those are the parts of the college experience others might enjoy most. But Agbonkonkon wouldn't have it any other way. He's been given an opportunity to build the world he always imagined.

"I'll tell myself, 'Why am I partaking in other people's universes when mine is still yet to be built?'" Agbonkonkon said. "Just having that mentality of: These are the things that I want to achieve, these are the things I'm willing to do to achieve it. The investment I put in now is going to pay dividends in the future."

This article originally appeared on For The Win: How Texas high jumper Osawese Agbonkonkon wants to clear the bar as a sci-fi author

title: High School Student Stunned To Find a Massive Pit Viper Hiding in His Football Helmet
description: A football player in Arkansas got the shock of a lifetime recently when he was at practice. The player had been wearing his headgear while participating in warm-ups when he felt something unusual in his ... Read more
fullText:
A football player in Arkansas got the shock of a lifetime recently when he was at practice. The player had been wearing his headgear while participating in warm-ups when he felt something unusual in his helmet, according to ESPN. But he didn't see anything amiss at first, so he brought the helmet to his assistant coach to take a closer look.

It was then that the Maumelle High School player learned that the strange feeling he'd been experiencing while on the field was thanks to a massive cottonmouth snake. The venomous reptile had apparently been snuggled up behind the padding. It began to move around during the warm-up activities.

ABC30 Action News reports that the pit viper wasn't exactly ready to give up his warm and snuggly hiding spot, so reinforcements were called in to help free and relocate the snake.

Fortunately, neither the snake nor the football player was injured during the incident, which remains a miracle in itself given the close quarters the pair briefly shared.

The high school student had been wearing his helmet for about an hour when he sensed something was wrong, according to Fox16. After his assistant coach discovered the pit viper—pit viper is another term used to describe the snake, which belongs to the viper family—the player reportedly grabbed a fresh helmet and continued with practice.

However, the coaches couldn't get the snake out of the helmet and were forced to call for help.

According to a Facebook post from Maumelle Animal Shelter, officials responded to the call for help, taking photos of the situation after they arrived. The pictures show just how deeply hidden the snake was in the helmet, explaining how the high school student could've initially missed the venomous hitchhiker.

"It was unreal," Animal Services Director Chris Davis told Fox16. "You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real."

Davis' group took the opportunity to remind people of the importance of checking their accessories and bags before they pick them up or put them on using those very same photos. "Thankfully, everyone is okay, but this is an important reminder that snakes and other critters can find their way into dark, enclosed spaces—especially helmets, shoes, bags, boxes, and other items that are left outside or sitting undisturbed," they wrote in part of the caption for the photos.

According to reports, the head coach also finished practice by sharing the same warning with players, reminding them that the pre-practice safety check should always involve checking equipment for potential hazards, which apparently now also includes cottonmouth snakes.

And with good reason, since the cottonmouth snake is the second most venomous snake in the state. Not only that, but Poison Control says that a cottonmouth snake's bite can be very painful. Recovery can take several weeks in some cases. People who have severe reactions to the bite could also need an antivenom, which can help slow or stop swelling at the site of the bite.

Hopefully this team has had its last run-in with snakes in helmets, but you have to imagine that everyone is going to be a little more vigilant when it comes time to put on the football gear in the future, thanks to this incident.

title: Next Jordyn Tyson? Former Colorado WR hopes to follow same path at ASU
description: During his time in Tempe, Jordyn Tyson blossomed into a first-round NFL draft pick after coming from Colorado. Another ex-Buff wants to do the same.
fullText:
Hines Ward knows there is no replacing Jordyn Tyson.

Tyson is a one-of-one. After coming over from Colorado following a serious injury as a freshman, Tyson blossomed into a first-round NFL draft pick under the guidance of Ward as the wide receivers coach at Arizona State.

"You know, there'll never be another JT," Ward told The Arizona Republic at its annual trip to Payson for Camp Tontozona.

But there's no denying the connections that some will make with another former Colorado Buff now in the ASU receiver room: Omarion Miller. In the offseason, Miller made the move from Boulder to Tempe via the transfer portal, following the same path as Tyson in 2023.

While Ward said Tyson is a unique player, he sees similarities between the two.

"Both competitors. JT, he hates losing. He hates any DB covering him one time and talking trash to him. He wants to redo it right then and there. Similarities are the same. Always extremely competitive, wants to win every time. He wants to make sure he's in the right spot making plays. I try not to compare people. People have their own little style to them."

Echoing what he said about Tyson, Ward ended his answer with, "There'll probably never be another Omarion."

The connections between Miller and Tyson extend further. During his visit to Colorado, Miller was hosted by none other than Tyson.

When Tyson made the move to ASU, Miller kept tabs on him. While he was busy with his own season at Colorado, Miller couldn't help but notice how well Tyson was doing with the Sun Devils.

"I definitely watched him during our season, being that during that season he was one of the better receivers in that class, so I kept an eye on him," Miller told The Republic. "Happy for him, he's in the league doing what he can. Wish I would have got a chance to play with him."

Seeing what Ward and the coaching staff did with Tyson, turning him "into an overall receiver," is what drew Miller to the school.

"Once he came here, the three years, the development that I've seen him change from was eye-catching to me," Miller said.

Miller is coming off his best season yet at the college level, with 45 receptions for 808 yards and eight touchdowns in 2025. He was regarded as a four-star transfer prospect and was seen as one of the biggest additions of the offseason for ASU. Miller was named to the All-Big 12 preseason team for the upcoming season.

At 6-foot-2 and weighing 215 pounds, Miller's build is similar to Tyson (6-foot-2, 200). Miller has the speed to break away from defenders but can also take a hit across the middle of the field with his frame.

"Very elusive," Ward said. "For his size, to be able to move, to be able to run, to change direction, and then, of course, exceptional ball skills. Watching him when we played Colorado last year, it just stood out on tape. I'm extremely happy to work with somebody with his skill set. He's just an all-around football player. I'm giving him the blueprints. Hopefully, he can go out there and help win some games for us."

Miller has drawn the attention of coach Kenny Dillingham, who recently said at Camp T, "He's been great. He's pushed himself a lot this camp."

At this time last year, Miller said he viewed himself mainly as an "X" receiver, the position that lines up on the outside. But Miller now feels like he is an "all-around" wide receiver who can play anywhere on the field.

It's been part of Miller's growth, both on and off the field, after joining the Sun Devils.

"O's a special dude," offensive coordinator Marcus Arroyo said. "Obviously, we all know about the skill set, right? I think his best attributes are, probably, the person. That's the piece you don't know about when you go out and you're in the transfer portal. You try to do the best background you can. But until you fuse them into your culture, you really don't know what's going to take shape.

"And he is a beautiful human. Awesome young man. Loves to work on and off the field. Carries the standards, carries our identity as an offense and a culture to the utmost. He does all the skill set stuff we know about. He hasn't been very long, and he's totally committed to being part of our culture and our team that fast. That's exactly what you hope to get."

Ward said Miller has grown tremendously since coming to Tempe in January. Players gravitate toward Miller and he's already become a key piece of the locker room. A viral video in March of a Miller one-handed catch on a punt certainly helped.

Not a single snap has been played yet for 2026. But Ward has a way of looking ahead. Only a few months after being hired at ASU, Ward said about Tyson, "We haven't scratched the surface of how good he can really be as an individual and as a football player."

Ward feels similarly about Miller.

"His ceiling's so high, all the abilities there," Ward said. "He can play at the next level. Now, it's just honing in the good habits, understanding what it takes to get to that level, to take care of your body, to jump in the playbook, what you do on a daily basis, basically being a pro at it. He's learned, he's grown since January. But all I've seen is taking strides and taking steps forward."

Logan Stanley is a sports reporter with The Arizona Republic who primarily focuses on high school, college and Olympic sports. To suggest ideas for human-interest stories and other news, reach out to Stanley at logan.stanley@usatodayco.com or 707-293-7650. Follow him on X, formerly Twitter: @LSscribe.

title: Kolt Dieterich proving his versatility for Washington football
description: The Washington Huskies have found a versatile piece for their offensive line in transfer Kolt Dieterich.
fullText:
As senior center Landen Hatchett continues to work his way back from a broken wrist, the Washington Huskies have found a new man in the middle.

In his stead, Jedd Fisch and offensive line coach Michael Switzer have turned to Sam Houston State transfer Kolt Dieterich at the position. Even though the Huskies initially added him to the roster out of the transfer portal to compete with freshman Kodi Greene at left tackle, the former five-star cemented himself in the starting lineup with a strong showing at spring practice after Dieterich was unable to participate in the spring with an injury.

That caused the Huskies to search for other ways to get the four-star transfer on the field, with center being the option that made the most sense following Zach Henning's transfer to Arizona and an arm injury to seventh-year Geirean Hatchett.

Dieterich began snapping in the spring, and following a few botched snaps during Washington's first team drills on Sunday, he has asserted himself as the team's starting center for the time being.

"I just kind of woke up one morning and said to Switz, 'Why don't we just get Kolt snapping?'" Fisch said of placing the Sam Houston State transfer in the middle.

"Now he's gotten himself to a spot where he's our starting center. And then when Landen gets back, now we've got opportunities to put Kolt really anywhere, but that kid is doing a phenomenal job."

Even with a few botched snaps along the way, the Huskies have been very pleased with Dieterich's progress with the position change.

"You got a fat guy right across the line of scrimmage from you, and he's about ready to knock you back," senior offensive analyst Matt Cavanaugh said of the difficulty of transitioning to center. "And then you're thinking about, 'Oh, I got to make a call,' and 'I got to tell the left guard to come with me,' or the right guard, and all of a sudden, the quarterback's giving you the cadence, and that snap's got to be perfect."

"He did a great job in terms of attacking that," Switzer added, stating that Dieterich has moved ahead of sophomore Jake Flores on the depth chart. "He's done some really nice things for a guy that never played the position...He's doing some good things. Are there things we need to work on? Absolutely."

title: Shelburne: Josh Kushner, Bob Iger will still 'Dodgerize' the Lakers
description: According to Ramona Shelburne of ESPN, the current process of "Dodgerizing" the Lakers that started under majority owner Mark Walter won't stop.
fullText:
One of the biggest questions surrounding the pending sale of Mark Walter's majority share of the Los Angeles Lakers to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger is how the franchise will be run by the two new incoming owners.

Walter had officially purchased his majority share of the Lakers this past October. Since then, he has looked to at least somewhat mimic how he has run the Los Angeles Dodgers, the two-time defending World Series champions, since he bought them in 2012. To that end, he brought in Farhan Zaidi and Andrew Friedman, two Dodgers executives, to handle some front office tasks for the Purple and Gold, and he has hired other capable men to prominent front office positions.

Perhaps not much will change with Kushner and Iger in charge, at least not at first. Ramona Shelburne of ESPN implied to Stephen A. Smith while on "The Stephen A. Smith Show" that both men will continue to "Dodgerize" the Lakers, at least for now.

"They were in the process of 'Dodgerizing' the Lakers. All of the brains and all of the apparatus that had been installed with the Dodgers to make them the most successful franchise in baseball the last few years was being implemented with the Lakers. ... Everyone who's been hired, everyone who's been put in place here, they're still going to keep doing what they're doing."

When Walter bought the Dodgers, they had been something of a Major League Baseball laughingstock, or at least a dormant franchise, for at least 20 years after being an iconic franchise from the 1950s to the 1980s. Under his leadership, the team quickly became a fixture in the playoffs and has finished first in the National League West 12 of the last 13 seasons while winning three of the last six World Series championships.

The Lakers, of course, won the NBA championship in 2020 with LeBron James and Anthony Davis, but since then, they have won a total of three playoff series. With James and several other rotation players from last season's roster gone, the team has done a solid job of remodeling its roster and surrounding Luka Doncic with a younger, speedier and more balanced cast.

The sale of the franchise isn't expected to become official until several weeks from now, as the NBA board of governors has to approve the transaction.

title: WWE SmackDown takeaways: Jacy Jayne, MFT win titles on stacked episode
description: Check out the top takeaways from WWE SmackDown on Aug. 14, 2026, which took place in Boston.
fullText:
WWE SmackDown on Aug. 14, 2026, took place at TD Garden in Boston and featured what was to be a singles match between Cody Rhodes and Sami Zayn.

This week's show was stacked with championship matches and all the big names you'd want to see on a Friday evening. CM Punk and Kevin Owens went at it in a promo segment, recapping their 20-year history in the business before they meet for the Undisputed title next week. It was easily the best episode of SmackDown in a long time.

Here's the top takeaways from this week's show:

Starting off the show were SmackDown GM Nick Aldis and Chelsea Green, who suffered a shoot broken orbital last week. As a result, Aldis called Green to the ring to ask her to relinquish the title. That request was met with a heartfelt response from Green, who ended up flipping the script on Aldis, tugging on his heart strings by bringing up both of their moments at SummerSlam.

Even though Green said until someone takes the belt from her, she handed the title over to Aldis and left the ring – but was stopped during her walk toward the back. Aldis changed his mind, and said Green has 30 days to figure out a way to defend the title, with a facemask, if necessary.

WOW 👏

Nick Aldis is giving @ImChelseaGreen 30 days to get healthy and defend the Women's WWE Title! pic.twitter.com/CsH8FDQTa1

The opening segment ended up with multiple layers, as Green's celebration of keeping the title turned into an interruption from Gunther, which prompted Matt Cardona coming out to defend his wife, which led to Gunther dominating him in a match, which then led to Nia Jax and Lash Legend coming to the ring, which led to Tiffany Stratton running out to save Green, which led to Stratton getting squashed.

Matt Cardona had heard ENOUGH! 👊@TheMattCardona pic.twitter.com/JJQfmUBHLC

The main takeaway here is that Green gets to keep the title. All of this fit her character very well. Rhea Ripley wasn't given a time limit to defend her title when she got injured – they just made an interim title match. But for Green, whose back is always against the wall, it made sense for Green to be pressed harder to defend. Regardless of the unfairness, the underdog Green got a small win here, which was good to see.

In the first of three championship matches, Baron Corbin put his still-white-furred US title on the line against Carmelo Hayes.

Out of the four matches on the card, this one was the best for back-and-forth action. Hayes and Corbin meshed well as a tall powerhouse against a speedy high-flyer, and the crowd appreciated what they displayed. Hayes looked to have it in the bag after hitting back-to-back First 48s, but Corbin rallied to hit an End of Days for the pin.

END OF DAYS 😵

Baron Corbin defeats Carmelo Hayes and retains the United States Title! pic.twitter.com/ZgJSgtuhxJ

After the match, Trick Williams entered, complete with spinning lightbox and all. While this distracted Corbin, Lil Yachty attacked from behind, and got outta there before Corbin could get his hands on him. Williams landed a Trick Shot Knee, and that was that.

That is a TRICK SHOT! pic.twitter.com/h0ELK44F5m

One of these days, Hayes will get another title run, but it just didn't make sense for Corbin to drop the title just yet, especially when it still has Williams' white fur all over it. It's obvious Corbin and Williams aren't done yet, and when they meet again, we'll find out how big this Corbin push truly is.

The second championship match of the night was a triple threat tag with R-Truth and Damian Priest putting their titles on the line against MFT and War Raiders.

The match was a chaotic mess of bodies all over the place. There were some fun double-team spots in and out of the ring, but the MFT, with Haku ringside, got the job done after hitting their double-team finisher, called The Brothers' Keeper. Haku joined them in the ring to hit the power pose with their new titles.

We have NEW WWE Tag Team Champions! 🏆

With Haku by their side, the MFTs have stormed to the Titles! pic.twitter.com/7VUy6VEs1t

Even though WWE recently hit a hard swerve in its incredible tag team scene, putting the titles on MFT with Haku could turn things around with a menacing heel duo on top. R-Truth and Priest were a fun babyface team, but their time was long overdue.

The third and final match of the night was for the women's US title between Tiffany Stratton and Jacy Jayne. Stratton came into the match still compromised from the beatdown from Jax and Legend earlier in the show. Regardless, Stratton decided to defend.

With Fatal Influence ringside, Chelsea Green provided some support for Stratton. Jayne worked Stratton's injured ribs throughout the match, but that wouldn't have mattered had the champ kept her eye on finishing her opponent. The women's tag champs, Fallon Henley and Lainey Reid, distracted Stratton enough for her to decide to dive onto them on the floor instead of hitting her finisher on Jayne. That decision backfired when Jayne met her with a Rolling Encore when she re-entered the ring.

NEW WOMEN'S UNITED STATES CHAMPION 🏆@jacyjaynewwe has DONE IT! pic.twitter.com/ucvPD9dpMt

Fatal Influence is now draped in gold, and good on 'em. The trio came to SmackDown vowing to take over, and so far, so good. The heel group has been a breath of fresh air for the women's scene on Friday nights, setting themselves up for what should be a nice run with titles on their shoulders.

The main event of this week's show was supposed to be a singles match between Cody Rhodes and Sami Zayn, with No. 1 contender stakes on the line for Zayn. However, when he entered to join Rhodes in the ring, Randy Orton attacked from behind.

OH MY GOD 😱

Randy Orton is hearing VOICES IN HIS HEAD! pic.twitter.com/MrKhfn6DuK

Orton's attack was sustained, and the match never happened. Orton went on a rampage, sending Rhodes all over the place and even shoved a poor ringside worker face-first into the ground – like, really hard:

Really Randy? 😳 pic.twitter.com/t6O132IdJv

It all led to a familiar spot, with Rhodes' head placed on the steel steps, awaiting a chair shot. Rhodes managed to kick Orton in the junk to stop the chair shot and swapped positions. However, officials stopped Rhodes from getting the chair shot off.

An absolutely WILD ending to SmackDown! 🤯@CodyRhodes | @RandyOrton pic.twitter.com/RHdbmxpFWD

Zayn will have plenty more to complain about next week, and will probably end up ruining next week's title match between CM Punk and Kevin Owens. As for Rhodes and Orton, just let them keep beating the stuffing out of each other on-site for the next few weeks until we get them one-on-one at an upcoming PLE.

title: Josh Hazlewood makes Australian Test history, joins elite club with 300th wicket
description: Josh Hazlewood marked a significant chapter in his career by taking his 300th Test wicket, joining an illustrious group of Australian bowlers. This achievement underscores Australia's strength, with four bowlers each having over 300 Test wickets on the field together. This historic moment unfolded during the first Test match against Bangladesh in Darwin, with Hazlewood achieving his impressive 14th five-wicket haul as well.
fullText:
Josh Hazlewood reached a major milestone in his Test career on Saturday, becoming the ninth Australian bowler to claim 300 wickets in the format during the first Test against Bangladesh in Darwin.

The Australia quick completed the landmark on his way to a 14th five-wicket haul in Test cricket, adding his name to an exclusive list that includes Nathan Lyon, Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc.

Hazlewood's achievement has also created a remarkable first for Australian Test cricket. Australia now have four bowlers in their current playing group who have each taken at least 300 Test wickets. No other Test team has had four such bowlers play together after all of them reached the milestone.

The 34-year-old has reached 300 wickets while maintaining an impressive career average of 24.02. Among Australia's nine 300-wicket bowlers, only three have better figures: Glenn McGrath at 21.64, Pat Cummins at 22.21 and Dennis Lillee at 23.92, according to Cricinfo.

Hazlewood's latest landmark was accompanied by another standout performance with the ball. He took all four wickets that fell after lunch on the third day and finished with six wickets in Bangladesh's first innings.

After removing Mehidy Hasan Miraz to break Bangladesh's stubborn resistance, Hazlewood dismissed Ebadot Hossain to complete both his 300th Test wicket and his 14th five-wicket haul.

Bangladesh were eventually dismissed for 426, giving them a commanding 228-run first-innings lead over Australia.

The visitors' innings was built around a maiden Test century from Tanzid Hasan, while captain Najmul Hossain Shanto and Mehidy also contributed half-centuries. Mehidy then showed his value with the lower order, batting for almost 50 overs as Bangladesh stretched their advantage.

The strong batting display followed an impressive bowling effort earlier in the match, when Hasan Mahmud claimed six wickets to put Bangladesh in a dominant position.

Australia also made life harder for themselves in the field, dropping five catches and allowing Bangladesh's lower order to add valuable runs.

The result has left Bangladesh in a commanding position despite arriving in Darwin after a heavy defeat to a Cricket Australia XI in their tour game.

For Hazlewood, however, the third day produced a personal milestone that further underlined his standing among Australia's finest Test fast bowlers. His 300th wicket places him alongside some of the country's greatest names, while his 14 five-wicket hauls reflect the consistency he has maintained throughout his Test career.

fullText:

title: Fantasy football sleepers to target in 2026: 1 name from all 32 NFL teams
description: Here's a list of 32 fantasy football sleepers in 2026 to target in your daft -- that's one from every team in the NFL.
fullText:
We have officially reached fantasy football draft season in 2026! For some, that means summer is heading toward its end, but also HEY FOOTBALL IS COMING VERY SOON!

If you're starting your draft prep, now's the time you're starting to think about sleepers, some of whom we've seen in action as the NFL preseason gets underway.

That's what this annual list is for: A look at the sleepers from around the NFL, with 32 of them to mark on your cheat sheet as you start your draft prep soon or later this month.

It's worth noting: Some of the names below may not end up being sleepers by the time you're drafting. Still, you've got to start somewhere. Here's a look at the sleepers you should be thinking about this year:

How much do we believe in Jeremiyah Love as a rookie? The answer here is in Allgeier, who could steal some carries and red zone work. James Conner is still in Arizona (for now), so keep an eye out here. But I could see Allgeier having a role that goes beyond backup who could have a bigger role if Love goes down.

Who's the WR2 in Atlanta? It might be the 2026 third-rounder out of Georgia who could carve out a role after a solid start to training camp.

In 27 years of covering the Ravens, I’m not sure I’ve seen a rookie have a training camp quite like wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane.

Every day, Lane produces a highlight-making catch. And today, he has Derrick Henry leaping in the air in celebration. pic.twitter.com/o86oFdqfmj

Similar to Branch above: A wideout who went in the third round this past April and who has turned some heads in training camp.

There's always been a lot of IFs with him. IF he could get more passes his way, he'd turn all that athleticism into big fantasy numbers. Maybe this is the year? Worth taking a flier and maybe pairing him with another tight end if you believe in that philosophy.

We all loved what he did late last season. Can he carry that over into 2026? Isn't it worth finding out with a late pick?

We know: D'Andre Swift is solid. But Monangai is a good bet in case Swift gets injured. Plus, he could have more of a role than we think with Ben Johnson's history in Detroit with leaning on two running backs.

He could end up as the RB2 behind Chase Brown if he can beat out Samaje Perine. There aren't a ton of sleepers from this team, so we label him a mega-deep sleeper.

Here's a thought: What if Quinshon Judkins isn't as good as we think he is? What if the Browns need to go through the air late in games? What if Todd Monken likes to have his running backs catch passes a lot? Hmmm.

This is one battle to monitor this preseason. The winner gets the RB2 job behind Javonte Williams.

We know he can catch passes. We also know that J.K. Dobbins is there ahead of him and that there are questions about his health. We ALSO know that Jonah Coleman was drafted earlier this year. He might be a draft-and-stash candidate.

All this dude does is throw the football. Nothing wrong with that! Sure, he may not run, but he may end up on the fringes of top-12 QB. That's value!

Are we going to see the Packers let him cook? You'll draft him as your second quarterback, but maybe there's a world where he becomes a solid starter.

The Texans are looking for a second WR behind Nico Collins. And Year 2 wideouts are a thing worth investing in. Remember that he caught six TD passes last year.

Let's see: Michael Pittman Jr. is gone. Alec Pierce doesn't seem healthy at the moment. I see a breakout coming based on volume even with Tyler Warren there as well.

I don't care that everyone thinks he's going to be a sleeper candidate. He looked like the top receiver in Jacksonville -- the concerns about Brian Thomas Jr. and maybe Travis Hunter could be a thing for Washington's value, but I'm buying a later-draft swing at a player who finished WR4, WR16 and WR6 in Weeks 16-18 last year.

Obviously, Ashton Jeanty is the top name in Vegas, but Washington Jr. could have some serious upside if he gets to play. There was buzz out of the 2026 draft about him and he looked good in the first Raiders preseason game.

You do have to wonder if Kimani Vidal will get some run as RB2 in L.A., but in a Mike McDaniel offense, he could elbow his way in to Omarion Hampton's workload and maybe into the FLEX spot conversation.

It depends on how much you believe in Kyren Williams doing THAT for a third straight year. Williams has 36 TDs in the past three seasons to go along with at least 1,144 yards on the ground. But Corum could be used more in 2026 or could be a top-10 RB should Williams go down with an injury. A worthwhile sleeper either way.

He will run. We know that. But we could see him throwing more than we think, especially if Miami's defense struggles, and all of that paints an intriguing picture for him potentially piling up the points.

He won the battle against J.J. McCarthy and he's coached by Kevin O'Connell. Let's couple that with his history as a running QB and a pairing with Justin Jefferson. I'd bet he beats his ADP with ease.

I'm not a believer in TreVeyon Henderson and Stevenson was really good last season. He won't be an RB1 by any stretch, but he's good enough to best where he's being drafted and be your solid FLEX.

Another later-round quarterback who could break out given who he's throwing to and his underrated rushing volume.

Is Cam Skattebo completely healthy? If that's a question, you have to grab Tracy. He could also be on the field for passing downs for an emerging Giants offense.

This is one for deep keeper leagues: The Jets spent a first-round pick on him earlier this year, so he could be a talent in the future. But with an injury setback in training camp and the presence of Mason Taylor, he may be a breakout candidate next year.

It's possible he's WR2 right away, which means he could be in line for veteran's level work despite being a rookie.

Jaylen Waddle has more of a certain role, but we saw Kenneth Gainwell carve out a spot last year on the Steelers and be productive. Don't sleeper on Dowdle.

He caught seven passes in the team's first preseason game. And the wide receiver position in the Bay Area is WIDE OPEN behind Mike Evans. Hmmm.

Drafting the big play threat is a bet on him having a full offseason in Seattle under his belt after the trade from New Orleans brought him to the eventual Super Bowl winners. Will he see more volume this year?

Dude catches passes and was great on the ground in Pittsburgh. And it feels like Bucky Irving is getting less hype this year. I'd take a chance here in the hopes that he leapfrogs Irving.

Carnell Tate has arrived to join Calvin Ridley, but it's the former Giant I'm most intrigued by. Former Giants head coach Brian Daboll is now coaching in Music City, and their familiarity could lead to Robinson getting the ball a lot more than you'd expect.

Sometimes, a dependable vet can be a fantasy sleeper. He was surprisingly good in New England last year and as the man behind Terry McLaurin on the depth chart, Diggs could get enough work to be a WR3 type.

title: 'Devdutt Padikkal is god sent': India star hailed for dominating Sri Lankan spinners on Day 1 of 1st Test in Galle
description: With Devdutt Padikkal bringing up his maiden Test century amid much uncertainty in the Indian dressing room, fans and critics alike hailed him for his masterful batting on Day 1 of the 1st Test.
fullText:
'Devdutt Padikkal is god sent': India star hailed for dominating Sri Lankan spinners on Day 1 of 1st Test in Galle originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Devdutt Padikkal scored a maiden Test century on Day 1 against Sri Lanka in Galle.

The RCB and India star dominated the Sri Lankan spinners with a fluent innings at number 3.

Sanjay Manjrekar and fans hailed Padikkal's technique against spin.

With a dressing room demolished by injuries, India didn't look at their best as they came down to bat at the 1st Test match at Galle. After a timing error that got Yashasvi Jaiswal run out early on, many even thought that an innings collapse was waiting for them. Devdutt Padikkal single-handedly changed that.

The RCB star announced himself on the Test stage with a superb maiden century against the Lankans' spin attack. The left-hander seized his opportunity at number three to leave India in a commanding position.

MAIDEN TEST HUNDRED! 💯

A special moment on a special day for Devdutt Padikkal in Galle 🥳

Updates ▶️ https://t.co/M9LVyCAp8y#TeamIndia | #SLvINDpic.twitter.com/8x1HcYeFbA

Handed the crucial No. 3 role in place of the injured Sai Sudharsan, Padikkal responded with a composed and authoritative innings.

He reached his hundred off 134 balls, ending a long search for stability in a position India has struggled to fill. His knock came in only his return to the Test side, having last featured against Australia in November 2024.

Batting on a spin-friendly Galle surface, Padikkal looked completely at ease against the hosts' slow bowlers, driving India towards a big first-innings total.

MORE: 'What a mix-up!': Jaiswal run out after miscommunication with Rahul in Galle

Padikkal's innings stood out for the manner in which he handled Sri Lanka's spin-heavy attack, led by star spinner Prabath Jayasuriya. He combined watchful defence with fearless strokeplay, repeatedly using his feet to disrupt the bowlers' lengths.

The left-hander struck a particularly memorable blow when he danced down the track to launch the left-arm spinner straight down the ground for a massive six.

It was an innings of authority and control, exactly the assured presence India has craved at first drop. By the time he reached three figures, India had moved past 200 with only one wicket down, a platform that could yet yield a substantial total.

His hundred also came in the context of KL Rahul retiring hurt with cramps, making his contribution all the more valuable.

MORE: LIVE: India vs Sri Lanka 1st Test live updates, score, weather report, toss, win chances, result and highlights from Galle

The performance drew widespread praise, with former India batter Sanjay Manjrekar leading the tributes. He was particularly impressed by the youngster's all-round game against the turning ball. Manjrekar wrote, "Devdutt Padikkal is God-sent for India v. spinners. Excellent technique, both in defence and attack."

Devdutt Padikkal god sent for India v spinners. Excellent technique, both in defence & attack. 👏👏👏

Fans were equally captivated by his authority at the crease. One supporter posted, "Devdutt Padikkal is stepping out and launching it straight down the ground for a massive maximum. Leaving the left-arm spinner with no answers. Absolute authority at the crease."

Devdutt Padikkal stepping out and launching it straight down the ground for a massive maximum! Leaving the left-arm spinner with no answers. Absolute authority at the crease! pic.twitter.com/uwvlFn2rS1

Another tracked his progress through the innings, first writing, "Devdutt Padikkal is making his mark at No. 3 for India," before adding as he reached his fifty, "DDP announces himself at No. 3 in Tests. A solid fifty-run innings from Devdutt Padikkal."

DEVDUTT PADIKKAL MAKING HIS MARK AT NO.3 FOR INDIA 🔥 pic.twitter.com/AiPgP6njZg

A special moment involving the team management also caught the eye. One fan shared a picture of the dressing room, writing, "That moment means a lot. Captain Shubman Gill and head coach Gautam Gambhir are applauding Devdutt Padikkal after his terrific fifty. A special moment for the youngster on his return to the Test setup."

❤️ 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐌𝐎𝐌𝐄𝐍𝐓 𝐌𝐄𝐀𝐍𝐒 𝐀 𝐋𝐎𝐓! 🇮🇳

Captain Shubman Gill & Head Coach Gautam Gambhir applauding Devdutt Padikkal after his terrific fifty.👏

A special moment for the youngster on his return to the Test setup. pic.twitter.com/vqOX8nhiQ4

Fans know that when the stoic coach Gambhir comes down to applaud an innings, then it is one to be noted.

MORE: KL Rahul injury update: India opener leaves pitch retired hurt after Tea

There is a strong argument that this innings is exactly what India has been waiting for. The No. 3 position has been a revolving door since the retirements of Cheteshwar Pujara, and while India has experimented with the likes of Gill and Sai Sudarshan before giving the chance to Padikkal in this Test, so far it hasn't been looking like it was working.

But after his performance today, a technically sound left-hander comfortable against spin could finally bring some permanence to a problem slot. The bigger question is whether Padikkal can turn this breakthrough into a lasting run in the side. With both Rahul retired hurt and Gill gone cheaply by a misplaced shot, he remains India's anchor for the first innings.

India might have a habit of chopping and changing its middle order, but a maiden century in these demanding conditions is a powerful statement. If he kicks on, Padikkal may not just have won a Test match for India but also settled one of the team's most pressing selection debates for some time to come.

title: STL Studio – a free, self-hosted library manager for 3D print files
description: Local web app for cataloguing and browsing large STL/3MF model libraries. Features full-text search, tag filtering, variant grouping, 3D preview, metadata enrichment from Gumroad/Cults3D/MMF, and a...
fullText:
Free, open source, and self-hosted: a home base for a 3D print library that's gotten out of hand. Search, tag, group variants, and actually find that one file again instead of digging through nested folders.

📖 User documentation: the STL Studio Wiki is the canonical user guide.
🗺️ What's coming next: ROADMAP.md
🤝 Contributing: issues and PRs welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

Getting Started ·
Feature Guide ·
Scanning & Folder Structure ·
Troubleshooting

The wiki is generated from the in-repo docs/ folder. The
in-app Help page is maintained separately for concise, contextual guidance.

Built because I had too many STL files and no good way to keep track of them.
It's grown from a personal fix into something other makers, painters, and
hobbyists use too.

Go to the Releases page and download the file for your OS:

For testing the newest successful main build before a versioned release,
use the rolling Main Build prerelease on the same Releases page.

On Windows, run the installer and launch STL Studio from the Start menu.
The Electron app opens in its own desktop window. On Linux, mark the binary
executable, run it, and open http://localhost:8484 in your browser.

Windows will warn you the first time. STL Studio is not yet
code-signed, so SmartScreen shows "Windows protected your PC" with an
unknown publisher. Choose More info → Run anyway. This is expected for
every release today — see
Windows blocked the installer
for the full walkthrough, and
Verifying your download
if you want to confirm the file is genuine before running it.

Go to Settings and add the folder paths where your STL files live.

Click Scan Library — models appear within a few minutes.

Your library database is stored in your user data folder and survives app updates:

Linux note: You may need to mark the binary as executable before running it: chmod +x stl-studio-linux

Copy .env.example to .env and set your drive paths (forward slashes, even
on Windows):

STL_DRIVE_1 mounts at /mnt/drive1, STL_DRIVE_2 at /mnt/drive2. Both are
seeded as scan roots automatically on first boot.

Open http://localhost in your browser.

Click Scan Library to index your files.

Got models on more than two drives, or need to change mounts? See
docs/docker.md — Docker can't be configured purely from the
Settings page the way the standalone app can.

Prefer not to build? Pre-built backend and frontend images are
published to GHCR on every successful main build and every release — see
docs/docker.md → Pre-built images.

A folder is only indexed as a model if it contains 3D files.

The Paint Shelf is always available in the nav. Enabling Settings → Painting Guides additionally adds Guides (guide authoring/reading).

Paint Shelf — paint inventory: search/filter by brand, line, finish, and owned state, with color chips for swatches. Per-line code patterns (regex) validate paint codes on entry. CSV import/export in PaintRack format (by Courageous Octopus — not affiliated) with a diff preview (never a blind overwrite); optional Color column (#RRGGBB, "rgb(r,g,b)", or "hsv(h,s,v)") pre-populates swatches on import.

Color-match studio — match a reference photo against your shelf. A value ladder (shadow → mid → highlight ramp in the same hue family, anchored on the sampled mid-tone) plus a hue ranking (ΔE2000) and a labelled glaze/wash list, each with a confidence band — suggestions to confirm by eye, never auto-applied. Eyedropper: click the preview to sample a specific spot (skin, hair, leather), plus an automatic palette overview with the background excluded. Large photos are downscaled in-browser before upload.

Painting Guides — step-by-step guides tied to your Paint Shelf:

Windows packaging CI smoke-tests the generated NSIS installer end to end. It
qualifies custom and default install directories, Start-menu and desktop
shortcuts, repair/reinstall, packaged-app launch and restart, database
persistence, and uninstall cleanup while confirming user data is retained.
This is a packaging smoke gate, not a replacement for manual UI acceptance
testing on a clean Windows machine.

Release candidates also require the manually dispatched Installed Update
Smoke workflow, which verifies the published-bootstrap → candidate updater
path, installer replacement, relaunch version, and retained database state. See
docs/release-checklist.md.

Both frontend and backend are baked into their images — rebuild after any code change:

For backend development, the docker-compose.dev.yml overlay bind-mounts the
source and runs uvicorn with --reload, so Python edits take effect without a
rebuild:

(The base image runs without --reload — it's a dev-only flag.)

Tests run automatically on every commit via a Husky
pre-commit hook. After cloning, run npm install at the repo root once to wire it up,
then docker compose build backend so the pytest step has an image to run in.

Backend (pytest — runs in Docker, no local Python env required)

Every PR to main (and every push to main) also runs the suite via the Tests
workflow, so regressions are caught alongside the binary Build Check.

CI enforces regression floors against the current tested baseline: 88% backend
statement coverage; 62% statements, 58% branches, 54% functions, and 65% lines
for the frontend; and 48% statements, 83% branches, 86% functions, and 48% lines
for the desktop process. Coverage reports are uploaded as workflow artifacts for
14 days so changes can be investigated without weakening the gates.

Run the same coverage checks locally with:

GitHub Actions builds the Windows NSIS installer and Linux headless binary.

One-click release: Go to the Actions tab → Release → Run workflow, pick
patch/minor/major. It computes the next version, creates the tag, and builds
a draft GitHub Release. The workflow validates the complete asset set, generates
SHA256SUMS, and runs the installed-update qualification before publishing it.

Manual tag (alternative): git tag v1.2.3 && git push origin v1.2.3 triggers the
same build.

Every PR to main runs Build Check, which compiles both supported platform
artifacts (without releasing) so packaging breaks are caught before merge.

STL Studio started because I had a problem: way too many STL files and no good
way to keep track of them all. What began as a personal tool turned into
something I thought other makers, painters, gamers, and hobbyists might find
useful too.

If STL Studio has helped you organize your collection, rediscover forgotten
models, or simply spend less time hunting through folders, please consider
supporting the project through
Patreon or
Buy Me a Coffee.

Your support helps fund continued development, but it also helps keep resin in
the printer, paint on the hobby desk, and supports my family as I balance
software development, creativity, and caregiving.

There's absolutely no obligation—STL Studio is, and will remain, a passion
project. But every bit of support is deeply appreciated and helps me continue
building tools and content for the community.

Thank you for being here, and happy printing!

title: A Control Panel for Electronics Prototypes
description: A compact 3D-printed panel of buttons, toggles, a potentiometer and MOSFET-driven LEDs for quickly adding human controls to electronics prototypes.
fullText:
Every prototype needing human input starts with the same chore: wire loose
buttons, LEDs and a potentiometer before testing the interesting part. So I made
that recurring mess permanent.

This scrap-built, 3D-printed panel has four momentary buttons, two toggles, one
potentiometer and three LEDs. Ten controls and indicators connect to any
microcontroller through ordinary jumper wires. It is a reusable physical
interface I can bring to a prototype instead of rebuilding inside it.

One side of every button and toggle connects to common ground; the other reaches
a front header. With a microcontroller’s pull-up enabled, closing a control
pulls its input low.

The potentiometer exposes ground, its wiper and its other end, letting the
prototype choose the voltage across the track and feed the wiper to an analogue
input.

Each LED’s anode takes power from VIN while a MOSFET switches its cathode to
ground. The microcontroller drives only the MOSFET gate rather than supplying
LED current through a potentially weak GPIO pin. Current limiting must still
suit the LEDs and VIN.

These are simple circuits, but rebuilding them consumes breadboard space,
jumper wires and attention. Loose controls also make interaction testing
needlessly awkward, and every rebuild creates another chance to debug wiring
that has nothing to do with the prototype.

I found large switch consoles and boards for individual controls, but little in
the useful middle: fewer than a dozen mixed controls in a small,
microcontroller-agnostic package. This panel is bench infrastructure, not part
of the product under test.

Displays and joysticks would turn this into another development board. The aim
is to make common physical controls instant, not to add protocols, software and
application-specific behaviour.

I surveyed projects on the web, estimated the 90th-percentile count for each
ordinary control and took roughly half. I then adjusted the numbers for a
pleasant arrangement and removed specialty inputs. This was an informal guard
against feature creep, not a scientific measurement: enough for common
projects, without designing for every outlier.

Placement follows the hand. Frequently used buttons sit at the bottom, clear of
everything else. The taller, less-used toggles and potentiometer occupy the
middle, reducing accidental knocks. LEDs sit at the top, above the working hand,
where they remain visible.

The flat case has conic, continuously curved corners—a simple, pleasant shape
without the harsh curvature changes of ordinary rounded rectangles, like a
squircle. Flat sides allow compact storage or standing on an edge; flush
headers keep the front equally clean.

title: Agent-shell – vendor-neutral chat with AI agents in Emacs
description: Another month, another agent-shell update. If you missed the last one, have a look at the 0.63 update. While this post showcases the latest highlights...
fullText:
Another month, another agent-shell update. If you missed the last one, have a look at the 0.63 update. While this post showcases the latest highlights, the full list of changes is far chunkier than what we'll cover.

agent-shell is a native Emacs mode to interact with AI agents powered by ACP (Agent Client Protocol).

Since inception in September last year (yikes nearly a year), agent-shell has featured a shell-like experience, powered by comint mode. There's also viewport mode (via agent-shell-prefer-viewport-interaction), if you prefer a more focused experience, and now we have chat mode.

Chat mode fuses comint mode with a more traditional chat-like labelling experience.

We're living on the edge here, so chat mode is now enabled by default. Ok not really that edgy, it's fairly safe (powered overlays) and can be disabled entirely via (setq agent-shell-chat-mode-enabled nil). Chat mode itself is a minor mode, so you can always toggle it on and off via M-x agent-shell-chat-mode.

In the last post, we talked about making agent-shell less chatty with more grouping for the likes of tool calls and agent thinking, all collapsed by default. If that's far too quiet, you can expand by default via (setq agent-shell-activity-group-expand-by-default t). If you found these two settings either too quiet or too chatty, we now have a third alternative via (setq agent-shell-activity-group-expand-by-default 'latest). When set, only the latest grouped activity is expanded by default, and automatically collapsed when the agent moves on to something else.

I've become quite fond of this feature (thank you @nhojb for the PR), so yes. It's also enabled by default.

Queuing received some improvements. The related commands have been consolidated under agent-shell-prompt-queue.el. You can queue prompts while the agent is busy, then view, resume, or drop pending prompts via M-x agent-shell-prompt-queue, M-x agent-shell-prompt-queue-resume, and M-x agent-shell-prompt-queue-remove. The pending queue is now shown after each new submission.

M-x agent-shell-prompt-compose opens a dedicated buffer for crafting a prompt, and it's now more independent of the shell. You can invoke it from any buffer (it resolves to the right shell), C-c C-c sends and returns you to whatever you were doing (fire and forget), and C-u C-c C-c submits the prompt and immediately lets you craft another queued prompt.

Shell initialization may take a second or two, depending on what agent you're using, which meant you had to wait for initialization before you could start typing into your new shell. Unnecessary, so that's no longer the case. Shell prompts are now offered as soon as possible, so one can get typing.

While Markdown lists are easily digestible without special rendering, we can do better than that, so we now give them a better treatment with normalized padding, indentation, and of course, civilized bullets.

TAB navigation made it into agent-shell fairly early on. I love being able to TAB my way into any section in the buffer and press RET to toggle folding. That's great and all, but we can make the navigation experience richer by welcoming the likes of Markdown source blocks, links, and images to the navigation party. Why these in particular? They are all actionable by RET too, of course.

While you'd rightly assume RET opens links to local text files in Emacs and delegates to browsers when needed, Markdown source blocks and images get a similar treatment. While their respective RET actions may not be as obvious, we can certainly make them much more discoverable, so we now add hints. Landing point on an actionable item now echoes a hint of what you can do and which key does it (say, "Press RET to copy" on a source block, "Press + to enlarge" on an image, and so on). Hints are also shown on mouse over events.

While agent-shell offers agent-shell-markdown-image-max-width for customizing image sizes, it's fairly restrictive. Not all images are the same, so why force them all to fit within the same constraint? agent-shell-markdown-image-max-width continues to offer a preferred default, but you can now scale images differently by getting the agent to annotate Markdown images with Pandoc-style link attributes.

The attribute block goes right after the image, taking a width and/or height in pixels or percentages:

I may be sweating the small stuff here, but this was really grinding my gears. We have lovely Markdown table rendering, which I'm glad we do as LLMs aren't always great at producing perfectly aligned tables. In the best of cases, the LLMs align the table perfectly, but it's just too wide for our Emacs window. Luckily, our lovely rendering also wraps cells to make them fit into our window. The thing is, all that lovely rendering goes out the door the moment you either resize your Emacs frame or merely split your window, resulting in a monstrosity like this:

I know. I'm sweating the small stuff here, but hey we don't have to live like this. Emacs has all the hooks in the world, so let's track window changes and rejoin the civilized world.

On a much smaller scale, I also wanted auto resize for images, so here you have it…

While we can influence image size at render time, this can still generate undesirable image dimensions, so we can now rescale all images in buffer on demand.

Sometimes a hammer really isn't the right tool, so we can now also rescale an image at point.

Opening a local file (from a link, image, or @file mention) now routes through agent-shell-file-display-action, a standard display-buffer action you can customize. The default reuses a window already showing the file, or takes over the current one.

If you'd like a different window arrangement, you could do something like:

Following a local file link now pushes your origin onto xref's marker stack, so xref-go-back (M-,) brings you right back to where you were in your agent-shell, just like other Emacs jumps.

Foldable fragments now use agent-shell-ui-fragment-map and bind agent-shell-ui-toggle-fragment. If you're not a fan of the RET binding to toggle folding, you can now use your preferred binding.

If TAB is your jam, you can do something like:

If you prefer styling agent thoughts differently, a new agent-shell-thought-body face lets you do just that.

Streaming performance also received some love. Thanks to @suhail-singh for the profiling and improvements, and to @Scott-Guest and @claytharrison for the trace analysis and benchmarking in #757.

The "Available config options" section now displays possible values.

agent-shell-agent-configs can now be set to a function, letting you compute the available agent configurations dynamically rather than hard-coding a static list. The function is called on every access, so it stays current across code reloads.

Maybe you'd like to list only available agents. Here's a rough snippet.

agent-shell-subscribe-to now broadcasts an agent-message-chunk event, handy for external integrations that want to observe streamed output.

executable-find now works correctly on remote hosts (#742 by @CeleritasCelery), smoothing out TRAMP-driven remote agents.

agent-shell-hq joins the family, offering an interface for managing multiple agent-shell sessions.

If you peeked at the commit logs, you'll notice I've been working daily on agent-shell, keeping up with project inflow. Since last month, 27 issues have been closed and 13 pull requests merged. As of today, the backlog sits at 11 open issues and 5 open PRs (versus 13 and 4 last time around). If there's something you'd like me to prioritize, feel free to ping.

Vendor-neutral tooling matters more than ever, and there are a couple of ways to help keep agent-shell going. Some cost money, others just a click. All are appreciated ;)

agent-shell is just me, an indie dev, while the tools it competes with have well-funded teams behind them. Time spent on agent-shell is time away from work that pays the bills, so if it's useful to you, please consider sponsoring the project. And if your employer benefits from your agent-shell use, nudge them to chip in too, they can typically contribute at a scale individuals can't.

GitHub stars help with exposure, attracting new users and potential sponsors. Starring agent-shell costs nothing and can potentially help bring in more funding, so if you don't mind a couple of clicks, the project can really use another GitHub star.

Thank you to all contributors for these improvements!

Liking agent-shell? Would like to see it evolve? Consider sponsoring the effort.
